bigPicture.subtitle: The Throne Room, Described by a Man in Chains
bigPicture.thesis: If we had to summarize the Book of Ephesians in one overarching thought, it is this: God has already made you alive, raised you, and seated you with Christ above every power that will ever come against you — and everything He asks of you afterwards is not the price of that seat but the shape of a life lived from it.
paragraphs: Start with the name on the cover, because it is the strangest thing about the book. Every other letter Paul wrote is named after people with a problem — Corinth's factions, Galatia's legalists, Rome's uneasy mix of Jew and Gentile. This one is named for a city the letter itself never actually addresses: the words in Ephesus are absent from 1:1 in the earliest and best copies we possess, and later scribes filled the blank in. And the letter behaves exactly like a letter written with a blank in it. It corrects no crisis. It answers no opponent. It names no local sin. Out of six chapters it mentions one human being besides Paul — Tychicus, the man carrying it (6:21–22) — and this from an apostle who spent three years in Ephesus, longer than anywhere else Luke records. You have just finished a circular — a letter meant to be read out in one congregation and then walked on to the next, town by town across the province of Asia, every assembly hearing its own name in the gap. So the gap in verse 1 was never damage. It was an invitation, and for six chapters your name has been in it.

Now weigh what six chapters actually did to you, because the architecture only shows itself from the far end. Go back over chapters 1 to 3 and underline the subject of every main verb: He chose, predestined, freely gave, redeemed, forgave, made known, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, brought near, broke down, reconciled, built, indwelt. Fifteen actions, one actor, and you are what almost every one of them lands on. In three chapters of that you are asked for exactly one thing, and it is not a performance but a memory: "Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh" (2:11). Then comes the sentence that changes your position in the letter: "I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called" (4:1). Everything that follows rests on one word — therefore — and that word is load-bearing, not decorative. Take the imperatives of chapters 4 to 6 as the terms of your acceptance and the building comes down on your head. Take them as the ordinary conduct of a man who has already been given a seat, and every one of them turns out to be within reach. Six chapters have been drilling that order into you. It is the first thing to carry out of this book and the last thing to let go of.

And do not let anyone hand this letter back to you as a soothing devotional. Ephesus was the occult capital of the ancient world, a city whose converts burned their spell books in a public bonfire worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). To those people Paul writes about a real hierarchy of unseen authority and a Christ already seated "far above all rule, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come" (1:21). This is a book in which men are dead and get raised (2:1–6), in which a stone wall between two peoples who genuinely hated each other is not negotiated down but executed in a body (2:14–16), and in which the closing paragraph issues armour because "our wrestling is not against flesh and blood" (6:12). Paul's word there is πάλη (pálē, G3823), the grappling of two bodies locked together — a contest settled by grip and weight, at a range where nobody is a spectator. Keep that scale when you remember this book. Ephesians hands you a throne and a fight in the same breath, and it will not let you keep either one without the other.

Then remember who held the pen, because it changes the sound of every sentence in the letter. Three times in six chapters he tells you where he is (3:1; 4:1; 6:20), and the third time he welds together two words that have no business sharing a line: "for which I am an ambassador in chains" (6:20). Ambassador is πρεσβεύω (presbeúō, G4243), the accredited envoy of a sovereign — a man whose person was legally untouchable, because to lay a hand on him was to declare war on his king. Chains is ἅλυσις (hálysis, G254), a fetter. Rome has done to this envoy precisely what the law of nations said could not be done to him, and across six chapters he never once files a complaint about it. That is the book you have just finished — the highest description of the church ever written, dictated by a man who could not cross his own room without another man's arm coming with him.

map.intro: Ephesians is the fifth of Paul's thirteen letters as the canon arranges them, and it sits on a seam you can feel. Behind it are the letters written on the road with the dust still on them — Romans arguing the gospel out in full, First and Second Corinthians refereeing a church tearing itself apart, Galatians defending justification with a raised voice. In front of it are the letters written under guard. Ephesians is the door of the prison corridor. It is also the widest-angle book in the New Testament: it opens before the foundation of the world (1:4) and closes in the unseen realm where the war is fought (6:12), and in all that distance it never once stops to fix a local problem. Every other Pauline letter is a specific answer to a specific mess. Because this one is answering nothing, it is free to describe everything.

sections.title: The Prison Corridor: You Have Just Walked Into It
sections.body: Four of Paul's letters were written from custody, almost certainly in Rome around AD 60 to 62, and you are now entering all four together: Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Philemon — the Prison Epistles. Paul says it himself three times in the book you just closed (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Two of them left the cell in the same bag: Tychicus carries Ephesians (6:21–22) and Colossians, and travelling with him is Onesimus, a runaway slave going home with the little letter to Philemon in his hand. Set the four side by side before you begin, because each takes one wall of the same room. Ephesians: the identity of the church. Philippians: the joy of the believer. Colossians: the supremacy of Christ. Philemon: what all of it costs on an ordinary Tuesday, when "one new man" (2:15) stops being a doctrine and turns up at your door with a name, a history, and a debt you are being asked to write off. And do not miss the pattern that governs the whole corridor. The most exalted description of the church in the Bible was written from the most confined place in the New Testament. Where they put Paul had no bearing on where God had seated him.

sections.title: After Galatians: From Defending the Gospel to Furnishing It
sections.body: The Spirit put Ephesians here because a house cannot be furnished while it is still being fought over. Galatians is a rescue operation — no thanksgiving, a curse pronounced twice, an apostle resisting Peter to his face over a dinner table where the wall was quietly going back up one chair at a time. Ephesians is the residence. Galatians ends its great argument on a sentence it has no room left to open up: "So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ" (Galatians 4:7). Heir — and then the letter stops. Ephesians is where somebody finally reads the will out loud. κληρονομία (klēronomía, G2817), inheritance, surfaces three times in the first chapter alone: you were "assigned an inheritance" (1:11); the Spirit Himself is "a pledge of our inheritance" (1:14) — ἀῤῥαβών (arrhabṓn, G728), the deposit handed over in advance as legal security that the rest is coming; and Paul prays you would grasp "the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints" (1:18). And notice what Galatians never once says: not a single mention of the heavenly places. The ground floor had to be won before the upper floor could be described. Galatians proves that nothing may be added to the cross. Ephesians shows you what the cross added to you.

sections.title: The Letter With a Blank Where the Address Should Be
sections.body: It matters enormously that this book fixes nothing. Corinth got surgery. Galatia got a rebuke. Rome got an argument. Had Ephesians been written to put out a fire, we would forever read it as firefighting — every glorious sentence quietly discounted as an overstatement aimed at somebody else's particular problem. Instead the canon holds one Pauline letter that is pure architecture: no scandal to date it, no grievance to file it under, nothing in it that can be reduced to a local case. That is why the church has always reached for this book when it needs to know what it actually is rather than what it is currently doing — and why not one line of it can be dismissed as someone else's mail.

sections.title: Where This Book Sits in the Whole Bible's Story
sections.body: Step back far enough and Ephesians is Genesis answered. Genesis gives you a garden, a walk with God, then exile and a flaming sword barring the way back; Ephesians gives you access — "For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father" (2:18), and "in whom we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him" (3:12). Genesis 2:24 gives you a man leaving father and mother to become one flesh with his wife; Ephesians quotes that verse and then says something nobody saw coming: "This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly" (5:32) — marriage was always a signpost to a marriage. Psalm 110:1, the single Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes and echoes more than any other, seats David's Lord at God's right hand until His enemies become His footstool; Ephesians 1:20–22 cashes that psalm in, then does the unthinkable and seats you there too (2:6). Isaiah 59 shows the LORD looking for a man to intervene, finding none, and arming Himself instead — righteousness for a breastplate, salvation for a helmet (59:16–17); Ephesians 6 takes that same armour off God and buckles it onto you. And carry one sober postscript out of this book. A generation later the risen Christ dictates a short letter to the church at Ephesus (Revelation 2:1–7), commends its labour and its doctrinal vigilance, and then holds one thing against it: it has left its first love. The congregation that received the highest revelation of love in the New Testament is the one later warned about losing it. What you have just been shown, you must keep.

roadAhead.intro: The Road Ahead: Ephesians closes with a man in irons asking, of all things, for prayer that his mouth would be bold (6:19–20). The canon now hands you two more letters written from that same chain, in that same season, carried out of that same door. You have been told where you are seated. Philippians lets you hear what that seat sounds like when the cell door stays shut. Colossians turns the identical truth around and puts the spotlight on the One you are seated with.

books.connection: Same prisoner, same season, an entirely different room in the heart. Philippi was the church Paul planted in Acts 16 — Lydia the cloth trader, a slave girl set free, a jailer converted at midnight after two beaten men sang with their feet in the stocks — and it is the one congregation that never stopped sending him money. So watch what Paul does not do here. He corrects no doctrine. He disciplines no sinner. He answers no heresy of theirs. The sharpest pastoral moment in four chapters is asking two women to agree with each other. This is the imprisoned apostle writing to a church he simply loved, and the result is the warmest thing he ever wrote: the joy words — χαρά (chará, G5479) and χαίρω (chaírō, G5463) — land more than a dozen times in a letter composed under guard. Ephesians told you your blessings are stored "in the heavenly places" (1:3), where no thief, court, recession or diagnosis can reach them; Philippians is the man proving it with a capital trial pending. Then it shows you something Ephesians never does — the descent. Ephesians 1:20–21 gives you the ascent: raised, seated, far above every name that is named. Philippians 2 gives you the road He took to get there. He emptied Himself — κενόω (kenóō, G2758), to make empty, to pour out to nothing — took a servant's form, obeyed all the way down to a cross, and therefore God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name. And that mind is not admired, it is commanded: φρονέω (phronéō, G5426), to have this mindset among yourselves. Ephesians seats you in the heavenly places; Philippians tells you the way up is down. It lands on contentment in any circumstance — αὐτάρκης (autárkēs, G842), a word the Stoics used for self-sufficiency, which Paul empties out and refills with Christ. If Ephesians 3:20 is the promise, "Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us", then Philippians 4 is that power in working clothes: in a cell, on an empty stomach, still singing.

Colossians is Ephesians' twin, and you will feel it within a page. Written at the same time, carried by the same courier — Ephesians 6:21–22 introduces Tychicus, Colossians 4:7–9 introduces the same man arriving with Onesimus — and roughly a third of Ephesians' wording turns up again: the walk, the putting off and putting on, the psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, the redeeming of the time, the household code. But twins are not clones, and the difference is the key that unlocks both books. Ephesians exalts the CHURCH as Christ's body. Colossians exalts CHRIST as the body's head. Ephesians 1:22–23 finishes with your eyes on the body: "and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all." Colossians turns the telescope round. In Christ all the fullness of Deity dwells bodily — θεότης (theótēs, G2320), divinity itself, and σωματικῶς (sōmatikōs, G4985), bodily, physically — and He is the κεφαλή (kephalḗ, G2776), the head of the body, so that in all things He might hold first rank: πρωτεύω (prōteúō, G4409). And Colossians is aimed, because Colossae had a specific error Ephesus did not. Teachers there were adding to Christ — the worship of angels, visions somebody claimed to have had, festival and food rules, harsh treatment of the body — and Paul's verdict is one devastating word: all of it has a reputation for wisdom in ἐθελοθρησκεία (ethelothrēskeía, G1479), self-made, do-it-yourself religion, and it is worth nothing against the flesh. Ephesians warned you never to let chapters 4 to 6 become the ground of your acceptance; Colossians aims that same warning at every salesman who offers you a required extra — a technique, an experience, an intermediary, a diet, a hierarchy of spirits. And it hands you the practical conclusion of Ephesians 2:6: you were made to sit with Him in the heavenly places, therefore seek and set your mind — φρονέω again — on the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Ephesians gives you the address. Colossians tells you to think from it.

themesMastered.title: In the Heavenly Places — Five Sightings, One Address
themesMastered.body: Five times in six chapters Paul reaches for one phrase, and he never uses it anywhere else in the Bible: ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, from ἐπουράνιος (epouránios, G2032) — above the sky. There is no word for places in the Greek at all; translators supply it because English will not carry a floating adjective. So do not picture geography. Picture the level of reality where authority actually sits, the one that settles what happens down here. Now count the five. Your blessings are banked there: "every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ" (1:3). Christ is enthroned there, "far above all rule, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name that is named" (1:20–21). You are seated there: "and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus" (2:6). The church is put on show there, before "the principalities and the powers" (3:10). And the war is fought there, "against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places" (6:12). Five sightings, one location — and that single fact rewrites your strategy. If the treasury, the throne, your chair, the exhibition and the battlefield are all at the same address, then the fight was never about getting there. Which is why the closing command of this letter is never charge, never advance, never take: it is to stand against the wiles of the devil (6:11), to withstand and, having done all, to stand (6:13), "Stand therefore" (6:14) — ἵστημι (hístēmi, G2476), to hold the position you are already in. You now own this: a soldier who must capture the hill fights toward something. A soldier who has been handed the hill fights from it. You have been handed the hill.

themesMastered.title: But God — The Two Words That Cut Your Life in Half
themesMastered.body: This letter will not give you the mercy until you have countersigned the diagnosis, and the diagnosis is not flattering. "You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins" (2:1). Dead is the whole verdict — not struggling, not underperforming, not a decent man going through a bad stretch. And the dead in this chapter are not lying still; they are walking, "according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air" (2:2), and they are "by nature children of wrath, even as the rest" (2:3). By nature is the phrase that removes the last excuse. Not your upbringing, not your company, not a run of poor decisions — what you were. Then two words turn, and the whole New Testament turns with them: "But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us" (2:4). Rich is πλούσιος (ploúsios, G4145); mercy is ἔλεος (éleos, G1656), the compassion that gets up and does something. And what it did arrives as three verbs that Greek fuses to a single preposition — with: made alive together with Christ, συζωοποιέω (syzōopoiéō, G4806); raised us up with him, συνεγείρω (synegeírō, G4891); made us to sit with him, συγκαθίζω (synkathízō, G4776), to be given a seat in company with (2:5–6). Weigh what that means. A corpse is beyond encouragement — you cannot coach it, motivate it, or offer it a second chance, because a second chance is no use to the dead. It can only be raised. And every one of those three verbs has already happened to you: "for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast" (2:8–9). You now own this: accusation will always build its case out of verses 1 to 3, and it is usually not lying about the evidence. Its trick is to close the file before verse 4.

themesMastered.title: The Hinge Called "Therefore"
themesMastered.body: "I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called" (4:1). Worthily is ἀξίως (axíōs, G516), an adverb of matching weight — two things balancing on the same scale. Put a calling in one pan and a life in the other, and Paul is asking that they weigh the same. He is not asking you to earn the calling; the calling was issued, sealed and delivered across chapters 1 to 3, and 4:1 opens with therefore. The letter had already settled where your good works belong: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them" (2:10). Workmanship is ποίημα (poíēma, G4161), the finished article, the thing that came out of the maker's hands. Read the end of that verse slowly. The works were laid down in advance. You are not producing evidence to satisfy a court; you are walking a path that was surveyed before you arrived. Then watch how far down this heavenly letter is willing to reach, because a man seated above every power gets measured on the ground: "Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth" (4:29); "Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath" (4:26), a deadline on your temper set by the sunset; hands that work so that there is something to hand over (4:28); "redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (5:16) — ἐξαγοράζω (exagorázō, G1805), to buy it up out of the market before somebody else does; "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly" (5:25); your children (6:4); your work and whoever you answer to (6:5–9). The throne room and the kitchen are in the same letter on purpose. You now own the test, and it is a test of direction rather than of effort: the day chapters 4 to 6 start to feel like instalments you are paying on chapters 1 to 3, you are reading the book backwards — and a man reading it backwards ends up tired, religious, and quietly bitter about it.

themesMastered.title: One New Man: The Wall Is the Sermon
themesMastered.body: Herod's temple had a low stone fence around its inner courts with notices fixed along it, and the notices did not threaten a fine. They told any foreigner who stepped over that his death was his own doing. Two of those stones have come out of the ground and survive in museums today; the barrier was real, the wording was real, and the man writing this letter is in prison because a crowd swore he had walked a Gentile past it — Trophimus, from Ephesus, of all cities (Acts 21:29). So weigh what it costs him to write this: "For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition" (2:14) — μεσότοιχον (mesótoichon, G3320), a dividing wall. And weigh God's method, because it was not diplomacy. He did not talk two hostile peoples into tolerating one another; He put the hostility itself to death: "having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace" (2:15), "and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility thereby" (2:16). The outcome was not Jews absorbing Gentiles or Gentiles absorbing Jews. It was one new man — a category that did not exist on the morning of the crucifixion. "So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (2:19). Then chapter 3 tells you why God paid that price, and it will change how you hear the next church quarrel you sit through: "to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places" (3:10). Manifold is πολυποίκιλος (polypoíkilos, G4182), many-coloured, the word for a weave running in a dozen shades at once. God is making an argument in front of the powers, and the argument is not a doctrine. It is a room. Old enemies at one table is the exhibit. You now own this: when a congregation splits along race, class, tribe, tongue, denomination or family, that is not a difficult personality. That is an attack on the evidence.

experientialLesson.intro: How do you walk out the Book of Ephesians practically moving forward? Here is your experiential blueprint:

steps.title: Praying the Prisoner's Prayer
steps.lesson: The Lesson: Twice the letter stops dead and the chained man prays out loud (1:15–23; 3:14–21). Between them he asks God for a great deal, and not one item on the list is a change of circumstances. No release. No acquittal. No relief. What he wants is "a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him; having the eyes of your hearts enlightened" (1:17–18) — σοφία (sophía, G4678), wisdom; ἀποκάλυψις (apokálypsis, G602), an unveiling of what was already there; ἐπίγνωσις (epígnōsis, G1922), full recognition as against mere information. Then, on his knees, "that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inward man" (3:16). Set those two prayers beside your own and the contrast is uncomfortable. He is the one in irons, and he is praying for the eyesight of people who are free. Ephesians has been making one point about your prayer life for six chapters: a very large share of what you have been begging God to change would stop tormenting you if you could simply see what is already true.
steps.practice: The Practice: Write 1:17–19 and 3:16–19 out by hand on a single card and keep it in your Bible. For the next seven days pray both of them word for word — once over yourself and once over one other person by name — and put a hard rule on it: you may not ask God to change a single circumstance until you have first asked Him for sight. On the seventh day write one sentence at the bottom of the card: what do I now see that I could not see on day one? Do that, and you will have learned the discipline that produced this book — asking for revelation before rescue.

steps.title: The Two-Column "But God"
steps.lesson: The Lesson: When accusation arrives, this letter never tells you to produce a better record. It tells you where you are sitting. That looks like a strange defence until you notice that Ephesians argues that way itself — it spends 2:1–3 conceding the prosecution's entire case, then answers it with two words about God rather than one word about you: "But God, being rich in mercy" (2:4). Your defence is not that the charges were overstated. Your defence is that the accused was put to death, raised, and seated, and the file is closed. There are two ways to lose that, and most believers manage one of them. Some spend years auditioning for a seat they were given long ago, which is why a single bad week can feel like a verdict. Others take the seat and forget the war, and are then astonished every time they are ambushed. This book refuses you both: it seats you in chapter 2 and arms you in chapter 6, and it expects you to know that you are doing both at once.
steps.practice: The Practice: Take a sheet of paper and rule a line down the middle. Head the left column "What I was" and write it in the letter's own words and then in your own — the actual sins, the actual years, the name you would be ashamed to have attached to you in public. Head the right column "But God" and write the verbs of 2:4–6 with your own name inside them: He loved me, He made me alive together with Christ, He raised me up with Him, He made me to sit with Him. Sign it, date it, keep it in your Bible. Then use it. When the accusation starts, do not stand in the dock trying to out-argue it with your own record — read the right-hand column aloud and answer from the chair. Then, so that the seat produces a walk, take one command from the back half of the letter and put a measurable rule on it for thirty days: your mouth (4:29), the sundown deadline on your anger (4:26–27), your hands and your giving (4:28), or your use of time (5:16). One rule. Thirty days. That is what a seated man's walk looks like on the ground.

steps.title: Dressing Before Dawn — and Fighting the Right Enemy
steps.lesson: The Lesson: "Finally, be strong in the Lord, and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil." (6:10–11). Whole armour is πανοπλία (panoplía, G3833), the full panoply — everything, not a menu you are free to shop from. Wiles is μεθοδεία (methodeía, G3180), a method, a worked-out strategy, which is why your temptations are so precisely fitted to your weaknesses. Then the enemy is named with surgical precision: "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." (6:12). Read that list again and notice who is not on it. Not your spouse. Not your father. Not that colleague, that pastor, that tribe, that church member. Every hour you spend fighting flesh and blood is an hour the real enemy operates unopposed. And notice that the last instruction is not a weapon you swing but a posture you keep: "with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints" (6:18).
steps.practice: The Practice: Two acts, and do them both. First, a drill before the day starts — out loud, standing. Name each piece and where it lands today: truth buckled on (what am I refusing to lie about?), the breastplate of righteousness (whose righteousness am I standing in — mine or His?), feet fitted with the Good News of peace, then "the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one" (6:16) — name the darts out loud by their real names: fear, lust, accusation, discouragement — then "the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (6:17), which means one specific verse loaded in your mouth for the specific fight of that specific day. Second, the demolition. Name the one flesh-and-blood person you have been treating as the enemy. This week take one concrete step of nearness toward them — a meal, a phone call, an apology, a seat at your table — and then pray for them by name in the Spirit. Christ killed that hostility in His own flesh (2:16). Do not keep it alive in yours.

finalDeclaration: Father of glory, I take my seat. I declare what You have done, and I will not argue with it. Before the foundation of the world You chose me in Christ. You predestined me for adoption as Your child and freely gave me favour in the Beloved. In Him I have redemption through His blood and the forgiveness of my trespasses, according to the riches of Your grace. I am sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the pledge of my inheritance — and what You have sealed, no accuser may open. I declare the truth about what I was, so that I can declare the truth about what You did. I was dead in transgressions and sins. I walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air. I was by nature a child of wrath, even as the rest, with nothing in my hands and no case to make. But God — rich in mercy, for Your great love with which You loved me — made me alive together with Christ, raised me up with Him, and made me to sit with Him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. By grace I have been saved through faith, and that not of myself; it is Your gift, not of works, so that I cannot boast. I am Your workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works You prepared beforehand, that I would walk in them. So I stop auditioning. I stop paying rent on a seat You gave me. Jesus, You are my peace. I was far off; I am made near by Your blood. I am no longer a stranger and a foreigner, but a fellow citizen with the saints and of the household of God. You broke down the middle wall of partition and killed the hostility in Your own flesh — so I will not rebuild with my prejudice what You demolished with Your body. Every wall still standing in me, against any people, tribe, tongue, family or name I know, I call what You call it: rubble. Holy Spirit, strengthen me with power in the inward man. Let Christ dwell in my heart through faith. Root me and ground me in love, until I know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge and am filled with all the fullness of God. Then teach me to walk worthily of the calling with which I was called — patient with people I find hard, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, with a mouth that builds, a temper that does not outlive the sunset, hands that work so that I have something to give, and forgiveness measured out exactly as You in Christ forgave me. I will not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom I was sealed for the day of redemption. I walk in love. I walk as a child of light. I redeem the time, because the days are evil. And when the fight comes — and it is coming — my wrestling is not against flesh and blood. So I lay down every war I have been waging against people, and I take up the real one. I am strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. I put on the whole armour of God, all of it, not the pieces I prefer — truth, righteousness, the Good News of peace, the shield of faith against every fiery dart, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, in my mouth. I pray at all times in the Spirit, for all the saints. And having done all — I stand. Chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, sealed, made alive, raised, seated, brought near, built together: none of it was my achievement, so none of it is mine to lose. Now to Him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that I ask or think, according to the power that works in me, be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus, to all generations, forever and ever. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!
